<p><b>Pretty Good Privacy</b> (<b>PGP</b>) is an <a href="/wiki/Encryption_software" title="Encryption software">encryption program</a> that provides <a href="/wiki/Cryptographic" class="mw-redirect" title="Cryptographic">cryptographic</a> <a href="/wiki/Privacy" title="Privacy">privacy</a> and <a href="/wiki/Authentication" title="Authentication">authentication</a> for <a href="/wiki/Data_communication" title="Data communication">data communication</a>. PGP is used for <a href="/wiki/Digital_signature" title="Digital signature">signing</a>, encrypting, and decrypting texts, <a href="/wiki/Email" title="Email">e-mails</a>, files, directories, and whole disk partitions and to increase the <a href="/wiki/Security" title="Security">security</a> of e-mail communications. <a href="/wiki/Phil_Zimmermann" title="Phil Zimmermann">Phil Zimmermann</a> developed PGP in 1991.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-:0&#95;4-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-:0-4"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>4<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>
</p><p>PGP and similar software follow the <a href="/wiki/OpenPGP" class="mw-redirect" title="OpenPGP">OpenPGP</a> standard, whose current specification is <a href="/wiki/Request_for_Comments" title="Request for Comments">RFC</a> 9580. RFC 9580 obsoleted RFC 4880, the earlier OpenPGP message-format specification. Modern versions of PGP are <a href="/wiki/Interoperability" title="Interoperability">interoperable</a> with <a href="/wiki/GnuPG" class="mw-redirect" title="GnuPG">GnuPG</a> and other OpenPGP-compliant systems.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-5" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-5"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>5<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>
</p><p>The OpenPGP standard has received criticism for its long-lived keys and the difficulty in learning it,<sup id="cite&#95;ref-6" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-6"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>6<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> as well as the <a href="/wiki/EFAIL" title="EFAIL">Efail</a> vulnerabilities, which affected some email clients using OpenPGP or S/MIME.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-7" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-7"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>7<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup><sup id="cite&#95;ref-8" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-8"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>8<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> The new OpenPGP standard (<a href="/wiki/Request_for_Comments" title="Request for Comments">RFC</a> 9580) has also been criticised by the maintainer of <a href="/wiki/GnuPG" class="mw-redirect" title="GnuPG">GnuPG</a> <a href="/wiki/Werner_Koch" title="Werner Koch">Werner Koch</a>, who in response created his own specification LibrePGP.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-LibrePGP&#95;9-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-LibrePGP-9"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>9<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> This response was divisive, with some embracing his alternative specification<sup id="cite&#95;ref-10" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-10"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>10<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> and others considering it to be insecure.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-11" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-11"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>11<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>
</p>
<meta property="mw:PageProp/toc" />
<div class="mw-heading mw-heading2"><h2 id="Design">Design</h2><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Pretty_Good_Privacy&amp;action=edit&amp;section=1" title="Edit section: Design"><span>edit</span></a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></div>
<figure typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:PGP_diagram.svg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4d/PGP_diagram.svg/500px-PGP_diagram.svg.png" decoding="async" width="500" height="521" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4d/PGP_diagram.svg/1280px-PGP_diagram.svg.png 2x" data-file-width="1589" data-file-height="1656" /></a><figcaption>How PGP encryption works visually</figcaption></figure>
<p>PGP&#160;encryption uses a serial combination of <a href="/wiki/Cryptographic_hash_function" title="Cryptographic hash function">hashing</a>, <a href="/wiki/Data_compression" title="Data compression">data compression</a>, <a href="/wiki/Symmetric-key_cryptography" class="mw-redirect" title="Symmetric-key cryptography">symmetric-key cryptography</a>, and finally <a href="/wiki/Public-key_cryptography" title="Public-key cryptography">public-key cryptography</a>; each step uses one of several supported <a href="/wiki/Algorithm" title="Algorithm">algorithms</a>. Each public key is bound to a username or an e-mail address. The first version of this system was generally known as a <a href="/wiki/Web_of_trust" title="Web of trust">web of trust</a> to contrast with the <a href="/wiki/X.509" title="X.509">X.509</a> system, which uses a hierarchical approach based on <a href="/wiki/Certificate_authority" title="Certificate authority">certificate authority</a> and which was added to PGP implementations later. Current versions of PGP encryption include options through an automated key management server.
</p>
<div class="mw-heading mw-heading3"><h3 id="PGP_fingerprint">PGP fingerprint</h3><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Pretty_Good_Privacy&amp;action=edit&amp;section=2" title="Edit section: PGP fingerprint"><span>edit</span></a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></div>
<p>A <a href="/wiki/Public_key_fingerprint" title="Public key fingerprint">public key fingerprint</a> is a shorter version of a public key. From a fingerprint, someone can validate the correct corresponding public key. A fingerprint such as C3A6 5E46 7B54 77DF 3C4C 9790 4D22 B3CA 5B32 FF66 can be printed on a business card.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-12" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-12"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>12<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup><sup id="cite&#95;ref-13" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-13"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>13<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>
</p>
<div class="mw-heading mw-heading3"><h3 id="Compatibility">Compatibility</h3><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Pretty_Good_Privacy&amp;action=edit&amp;section=3" title="Edit section: Compatibility"><span>edit</span></a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></div>
<p>As PGP evolves, versions that support newer features and <a href="/wiki/Algorithm" title="Algorithm">algorithms</a> can create encrypted messages that older PGP systems cannot decrypt, even with a valid private key. Therefore, it is essential that partners in PGP communication understand each other's capabilities or at least agree on PGP settings.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-14" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-14"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>14<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>
</p>
<div class="mw-heading mw-heading3"><h3 id="Confidentiality">Confidentiality</h3><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Pretty_Good_Privacy&amp;action=edit&amp;section=4" title="Edit section: Confidentiality"><span>edit</span></a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></div>
<p>PGP can be used to send messages confidentially.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-15" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-15"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>15<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> For this, PGP uses a <a href="/wiki/Hybrid_cryptosystem" title="Hybrid cryptosystem">hybrid cryptosystem</a> by combining <a href="/wiki/Symmetric_key_encryption" class="mw-redirect" title="Symmetric key encryption">symmetric-key encryption</a> and public-key encryption. The message is encrypted using a symmetric encryption algorithm, which requires a <a href="/wiki/Symmetric-key_algorithm" title="Symmetric-key algorithm">symmetric key</a> generated by the sender. The symmetric key is used only once and is also called a <a href="/wiki/Session_key" title="Session key">session key</a>. The message and its session key are sent to the receiver. The session key must be sent to the receiver so they know how to decrypt the message, but to protect it during transmission it is encrypted with the receiver's public key. Only the private key belonging to the receiver can decrypt the session key and use it to symmetrically decrypt the message.
</p>
<div class="mw-heading mw-heading3"><h3 id="Digital_signatures">Digital signatures</h3><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Pretty_Good_Privacy&amp;action=edit&amp;section=5" title="Edit section: Digital signatures"><span>edit</span></a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></div>
<p>PGP supports message authentication through <a href="/wiki/Digital_signatures" class="mw-redirect" title="Digital signatures">digital signatures</a> to verify whether a message was actually sent by the person or entity claimed to be the sender. The sender uses PGP to create a digital signature for the message with one of several supported public-key algorithms. To do so, PGP computes a <a href="/wiki/Cryptographic_hash_function" title="Cryptographic hash function">hash</a>, or digest, from the plaintext and then creates the digital signature from that hash using the sender's private key.
</p>
<div class="mw-heading mw-heading3"><h3 id="Web_of_trust">Web of trust</h3><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Pretty_Good_Privacy&amp;action=edit&amp;section=6" title="Edit section: Web of trust"><span>edit</span></a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></div>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1353705441" /><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <a href="/wiki/Web_of_trust" title="Web of trust">Web of trust</a></div>
<p>Both when encrypting messages and when verifying signatures, it is critical that the public key used to send messages to someone or some entity actually does 'belong' to the intended recipient. Simply downloading a public key from somewhere is not a reliable assurance of that association; deliberate (or accidental) impersonation is possible. From its first version, PGP has always included provisions for distributing user's public keys in an '<a href="/wiki/Public_key_certificate" title="Public key certificate">identity certification</a>', which is also constructed cryptographically so that any tampering (or accidental garble) is readily detectable. However, merely making a certificate that is impossible to modify without being detected is insufficient; this can prevent corruption only after the certificate has been created, not before. Users must also ensure by some means that the public key in a certificate actually does belong to the person or entity claiming it. A given public key (or more specifically, information binding a user name to a key) may be digitally signed by a third-party user to attest to the association between someone (actually a user name) and the key. There are several levels of confidence that can be included in such signatures. Although many programs read and write this information, few (if any) include this level of certification when calculating whether to trust a key.
</p><p>The web of trust protocol was first described by Phil Zimmermann in 1992, in the manual for PGP version 2.0:
</p>
<style data-mw-deduplicate="TemplateStyles:r1244412712">.mw-parser-output .templatequote{overflow:hidden;margin:1em 0;padding:0 32px}.mw-parser-output .templatequotecite{line-height:1.5em;text-align:left;margin-top:0}@media(min-width:500px){.mw-parser-output .templatequotecite{padding-left:1.6em}}</style><blockquote class="templatequote"><p>As time goes on, you will accumulate keys from other people that you may want to designate as trusted introducers.  Everyone else will each choose their own trusted introducers.  And everyone will gradually accumulate and distribute with their key a collection of certifying signatures from other people, with the expectation that anyone receiving it will trust at least one or two of the signatures.  This will cause the emergence of a decentralized fault-tolerant web of confidence for all public keys.</p></blockquote>
<p>The web of trust mechanism has advantages over a centrally managed <a href="/wiki/Public_key_infrastructure" title="Public key infrastructure">public key infrastructure</a> scheme such as that used by <a href="/wiki/S/MIME" title="S/MIME">S/MIME</a> but has not been universally used. Users have to be willing to accept certificates and check their validity manually or have to simply accept them. No satisfactory solution has been found for the underlying problem.
</p>
<div class="mw-heading mw-heading3"><h3 id="Certificates">Certificates</h3><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Pretty_Good_Privacy&amp;action=edit&amp;section=7" title="Edit section: Certificates"><span>edit</span></a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></div>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1353705441" /><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <a href="/wiki/Public_key_certificate" title="Public key certificate">Public key certificate</a></div>
<p>In the (more recent) OpenPGP specification, <i>trust signatures</i> can be used to support creation of <a href="/wiki/Certificate_authority" title="Certificate authority">certificate authorities</a>. A trust signature indicates both that the key belongs to its claimed owner and that the owner of the key is trustworthy to sign other keys at one level below their own. A level 0 signature is comparable to a web of trust signature since only the validity of the key is certified. A level 1 signature is similar to the trust one has in a certificate authority because a key signed to level 1 is able to issue an unlimited number of level 0 signatures. A level 2 signature is highly analogous to the trust assumption users must rely on whenever they use the default certificate authority list (like those included in web browsers); it allows the owner of the key to make other keys certificate authorities.
</p><p>PGP versions have always included a way to cancel ('<a href="/wiki/Certificate_revocation" title="Certificate revocation">revoke</a>') public key certificates. A lost or compromised private key will require this if communication security is to be retained by that user. This is, more or less, equivalent to the <a href="/wiki/Certificate_revocation_list" title="Certificate revocation list">certificate revocation lists</a> of centralised PKI schemes. Recent PGP versions have also supported certificate expiration dates.
</p><p>The problem of correctly identifying a public key as belonging to a particular user is not unique to PGP. All public key/private key cryptosystems have the same problem, even if in slightly different guises, and no fully satisfactory solution is known. PGP's original scheme at least leaves the decision as to whether or not to use its endorsement/vetting system to the user, while most other PKI schemes do not, requiring instead that every certificate attested to by a central <a href="/wiki/Certificate_authority" title="Certificate authority">certificate authority</a> be accepted as correct.
</p>
<div class="mw-heading mw-heading3"><h3 id="Security_quality">Security quality</h3><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Pretty_Good_Privacy&amp;action=edit&amp;section=8" title="Edit section: Security quality"><span>edit</span></a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></div>
<p>To the best of publicly available information, there is no known method which will allow a person or group to break PGP encryption by cryptographic or computational means. Indeed, in 1995, <a href="/wiki/Cryptographer" class="mw-redirect" title="Cryptographer">cryptographer</a> <a href="/wiki/Bruce_Schneier" title="Bruce Schneier">Bruce Schneier</a> characterized an early version as being "the closest you're likely to get to military-grade encryption."<sup id="cite&#95;ref-16" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-16"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>16<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> Early versions of PGP have been found to have theoretical vulnerabilities and so current versions are recommended.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-17" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-17"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>17<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> In addition to protecting <a href="/wiki/Data_in_transit" class="mw-redirect" title="Data in transit">data in transit</a> over a network, PGP encryption can also be used to protect data in long-term data storage such as disk files.  These long-term storage options are also known as data at rest, i.e. data stored, not in transit.
</p><p>The cryptographic security of PGP encryption depends on the assumption that the algorithms used are unbreakable by direct <a href="/wiki/Cryptanalysis" title="Cryptanalysis">cryptanalysis</a> with current equipment and techniques.
</p><p>In the original version, the <a href="/wiki/RSA_(algorithm)" class="mw-redirect" title="RSA (algorithm)">RSA</a> algorithm was used to encrypt session keys. RSA's security depends upon the <a href="/wiki/One-way_function" title="One-way function">one-way function</a> nature of mathematical <a href="/wiki/Integer_factorization" title="Integer factorization">integer factoring</a>.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-18" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-18"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>18<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> Similarly, the symmetric key algorithm used in PGP version 2 was <a href="/wiki/International_Data_Encryption_Algorithm" title="International Data Encryption Algorithm">IDEA</a>, which might at some point in the future be found to have previously undetected cryptanalytic flaws. Specific instances of current PGP or IDEA insecurities (if they exist) are not publicly known. As current versions of PGP have added additional encryption algorithms, their cryptographic vulnerability varies with the algorithm used. However, none of the algorithms in current use are publicly known to have cryptanalytic weaknesses.
</p><p>New versions of PGP are released periodically and vulnerabilities fixed by developers as they come to light. Any agency wanting to read PGP messages would probably use easier means than standard cryptanalysis, e.g. <a href="/wiki/Rubber-hose_cryptanalysis" class="mw-redirect" title="Rubber-hose cryptanalysis">rubber-hose cryptanalysis</a> or <a href="/wiki/Black-bag_cryptanalysis" title="Black-bag cryptanalysis">black-bag cryptanalysis</a> (e.g. installing some form of <a href="/wiki/Trojan_horse_(computing)" title="Trojan horse (computing)">trojan horse</a> or <a href="/wiki/Keystroke_logging" title="Keystroke logging">keystroke logging</a> software/hardware on the target computer to capture encrypted <a href="/wiki/Keyring_(cryptography)" title="Keyring (cryptography)">keyrings</a> and their passwords). The <a href="/wiki/FBI" class="mw-redirect" title="FBI">FBI</a> has already used this attack against PGP<sup id="cite&#95;ref-19" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-19"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>19<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup><sup id="cite&#95;ref-20" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-20"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>20<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> in its investigations. However, any such vulnerabilities apply not just to PGP but to any conventional encryption software.
</p><p>In 2003, an incident involving seized <a href="/wiki/Psion_(computers)" class="mw-redirect" title="Psion (computers)">Psion</a> <a href="/wiki/Personal_digital_assistant" title="Personal digital assistant">PDAs</a> belonging to members of the <a href="/wiki/Red_Brigades" title="Red Brigades">Red Brigade</a> indicated that neither the <a href="/wiki/Italian_police" class="mw-redirect" title="Italian police">Italian police</a> nor the FBI were able to decrypt PGP-encrypted files stored on them.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-21" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-21"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>21<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup><sup class="noprint Inline-Template" style="white-space:nowrap;">&#91;<i><a href="/wiki/Wikipedia:Reliable_sources" title="Wikipedia:Reliable sources"><span title="The material near this tag may rely on an unreliable source. (June 2018)">unreliable source?</span></a></i>&#93;</sup>
</p><p>A second incident in December 2006, (see <i><a href="/wiki/In_re_Boucher" title="In re Boucher">In re Boucher</a></i>), involving <a href="/wiki/United_States_Customs_Service" title="United States Customs Service">US customs agents</a> who seized a <a href="/wiki/Laptop_PC" class="mw-redirect" title="Laptop PC">laptop PC</a> that allegedly contained <a href="/wiki/Child_pornography" title="Child pornography">child pornography</a>, indicates that US government agencies find it "nearly impossible" to access PGP-encrypted files. Additionally, a magistrate judge ruling on the case in November 2007 has stated that forcing the suspect to reveal his PGP passphrase would violate his <a href="/wiki/Fifth_Amendment_to_the_United_States_Constitution" title="Fifth Amendment to the United States Constitution">Fifth Amendment</a> rights i.e. a suspect's constitutional right not to incriminate himself.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-22" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-22"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>22<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup><sup id="cite&#95;ref-23" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-23"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>23<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> The Fifth Amendment issue was opened again as the government appealed the case, after which a federal district judge ordered the defendant to provide the key.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-24" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-24"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>24<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>
</p><p>Evidence suggests that as of 2007<sup class="plainlinks noexcerpt noprint asof-tag update" style="display:none;"><a class="external text" data-mw-original-href="//en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Pretty_Good_Privacy&amp;action=edit" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Pretty_Good_Privacy&amp;action=edit">&#91;update&#93;</a></sup>, <a href="/wiki/British_police" class="mw-redirect" title="British police">British police</a> investigators are unable to break PGP,<sup id="cite&#95;ref-25" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-25"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>25<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> so instead have resorted to using <a href="/wiki/Regulation_of_Investigatory_Powers_Act_2000" title="Regulation of Investigatory Powers Act 2000">RIPA</a> legislation to demand the passwords/keys. In November 2009 a British citizen was convicted under RIPA legislation and jailed for nine months for refusing to provide police investigators with encryption keys to PGP-encrypted files.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-26" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-26"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>26<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>
</p><p>PGP as a <a href="/wiki/Cryptosystem" title="Cryptosystem">cryptosystem</a> has been criticized for complexity of the standard, implementation and very low usability of the user interface<sup id="cite&#95;ref-27" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-27"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>27<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> including by recognized figures in cryptography research.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-28" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-28"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>28<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup><sup id="cite&#95;ref-2015&#95;marlinspike&#95;29-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-2015_marlinspike-29"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>29<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> It uses an ineffective serialization format for storage of both keys and encrypted data, which resulted in signature-spamming attacks on public keys of prominent developers of <a href="/wiki/GNU_Privacy_Guard" title="GNU Privacy Guard">GNU Privacy Guard</a>. Backwards compatibility of the OpenPGP standard results in usage of relatively weak default choices of cryptographic primitives (<a href="/wiki/CAST5" class="mw-redirect" title="CAST5">CAST5</a> cipher, <a href="/wiki/Cipher_feedback" class="mw-redirect" title="Cipher feedback">CFB</a> mode, S2K password hashing).<sup id="cite&#95;ref-30" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-30"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>30<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> The standard has been also criticized for leaking metadata, usage of long-term keys and lack of <a href="/wiki/Forward_secrecy" title="Forward secrecy">forward secrecy</a>. Popular end-user implementations have suffered from various signature-stripping, cipher downgrade and metadata leakage vulnerabilities which have been attributed to the complexity of the standard.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-31" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-31"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>31<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>
</p>
<div class="mw-heading mw-heading2"><h2 id="History">History</h2><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Pretty_Good_Privacy&amp;action=edit&amp;section=9" title="Edit section: History"><span>edit</span></a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></div>
<div class="mw-heading mw-heading3"><h3 id="Early_history">Early history</h3><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Pretty_Good_Privacy&amp;action=edit&amp;section=10" title="Edit section: Early history"><span>edit</span></a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></div>
<p><a href="/wiki/Phil_Zimmermann" title="Phil Zimmermann">Phil Zimmermann</a> created the first version of PGP encryption in 1991. The name, "Pretty Good Privacy" was inspired by the name of a <a href="/wiki/Grocery" class="mw-redirect" title="Grocery">grocery</a> store, "Ralph's Pretty Good Grocery", featured in radio host <a href="/wiki/Garrison_Keillor" title="Garrison Keillor">Garrison Keillor</a>'s fictional town, <a href="/wiki/Lake_Wobegon" title="Lake Wobegon">Lake Wobegon</a>.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-32" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-32"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>32<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> This first version included a <a href="/wiki/Symmetric-key_algorithm" title="Symmetric-key algorithm">symmetric-key algorithm</a> that Zimmermann had designed himself, named <a href="/wiki/BassOmatic" title="BassOmatic">BassOmatic</a> after a <i><a href="/wiki/Saturday_Night_Live" title="Saturday Night Live">Saturday Night Live</a></i> sketch. Zimmermann had been a long-time <a href="/wiki/Anti-nuclear_movement" title="Anti-nuclear movement">anti-nuclear activist</a>, and created PGP encryption so that similarly inclined people might securely use <a href="/wiki/Bulletin_board_system" title="Bulletin board system">BBSs</a> and securely store messages and files. No license fee was required for its non-commercial use, and the complete <a href="/wiki/Source_code" title="Source code">source code</a> was included with all copies.
</p><p>In a posting of June 5, 2001, entitled "PGP Marks 10th Anniversary",<sup id="cite&#95;ref-33" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-33"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>33<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> Zimmermann describes the circumstances surrounding his release of PGP:
</p>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1244412712" /><blockquote class="templatequote"><p>It was on this day in 1991 that I sent the first release of PGP to a couple of my friends for uploading to the Internet. First, I sent it to Allan Hoeltje, who posted it to Peacenet, an ISP that specialized in grassroots political organizations, mainly in the peace movement. Peacenet was accessible to political activists all over the world. Then, I uploaded it to Kelly Goen, who proceeded to upload it to a Usenet newsgroup that specialized in distributing source code. At my request, he marked the Usenet posting as "US only". Kelly also uploaded it to many BBS systems around the country. I don't recall if the postings to the Internet began on June 5th or 6th.
It may be surprising to some that back in 1991, I did not yet know enough about Usenet newsgroups to realize that a "US only" tag was merely an advisory tag that had little real effect on how Usenet propagated newsgroup postings. I thought it actually controlled how Usenet routed the posting. But back then, I had no clue how to post anything on a newsgroup, and didn't even have a clear idea what a newsgroup was.</p></blockquote>
<p>PGP found its way onto the <a href="/wiki/Internet" title="Internet">Internet</a> and rapidly acquired a considerable following around the world. Users and supporters included dissidents in totalitarian countries (some affecting letters to Zimmermann have been published, some of which have been included in testimony before the US Congress), <a href="/wiki/Civil_libertarians" class="mw-redirect" title="Civil libertarians">civil libertarians</a> in other parts of the world (see Zimmermann's published testimony in various hearings), and the 'free communications' activists who called themselves <a href="/wiki/Cypherpunk" title="Cypherpunk">cypherpunks</a> (who provided both publicity and distribution); decades later, <a href="/wiki/CryptoParty" title="CryptoParty">CryptoParty</a> activists did much the same via <a href="/wiki/Twitter" class="mw-redirect" title="Twitter">Twitter</a>.
</p>
<div class="mw-heading mw-heading3"><h3 id="Criminal_investigation">Criminal investigation</h3><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Pretty_Good_Privacy&amp;action=edit&amp;section=11" title="Edit section: Criminal investigation"><span>edit</span></a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></div>
<p>Shortly after its release, PGP encryption found its way outside the <a href="/wiki/United_States" title="United States">United States</a>, and in February 1993 Zimmermann became the formal target of a criminal investigation by the US Government for "<a href="/wiki/United_States_Munitions_List" title="United States Munitions List">munitions</a> export without a license". At the time, cryptosystems using keys larger than <a href="/wiki/40-bit_encryption" title="40-bit encryption">40 bits</a> were considered munitions within the definition of the <a href="/wiki/Export_of_cryptography_in_the_United_States#PC_era" class="mw-redirect" title="Export of cryptography in the United States">US export regulations</a>; PGP has never used keys smaller than 128 bits, so it qualified at that time. Penalties for violation, if found guilty, were substantial. After several years, the investigation of Zimmermann was closed without filing criminal charges against him or anyone else in 1996.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-34" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-34"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>34<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>
</p><p>Zimmermann challenged these regulations in an imaginative way. In 1995, he published the entire <a href="/wiki/Source_code" title="Source code">source code</a> of PGP in a hardback book,<sup id="cite&#95;ref-zimmermann2&#95;35-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-zimmermann2-35"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>35<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> via <a href="/wiki/MIT_Press" title="MIT Press">MIT Press</a>, which was distributed and sold widely. Anybody wishing to build their own copy of PGP could cut off the covers, separate the pages, and scan them using an <a href="/wiki/Optical_character_recognition" title="Optical character recognition">OCR</a> program (or conceivably enter it as a <a href="/wiki/Type-in_program" title="Type-in program">type-in program</a> if OCR software was not available), creating a set of source code text files. One could then build the application using the freely available <a href="/wiki/GNU_Compiler_Collection" title="GNU Compiler Collection">GNU Compiler Collection</a>. PGP would thus be available anywhere in the world. The claimed principle was simple: export of <i>munitions</i>—guns, bombs, planes, and software—was (and remains) restricted; but the export of <i>books</i> is protected by the <a href="/wiki/First_Amendment_to_the_United_States_Constitution" title="First Amendment to the United States Constitution">First Amendment</a>. The question was never tested in court with respect to PGP. In cases addressing other encryption software, however, two federal appeals courts have established the rule that cryptographic software source code is speech protected by the First Amendment (the <a href="/wiki/United_States_Court_of_Appeals_for_the_Ninth_Circuit" title="United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit">Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals</a> in the <a href="/wiki/Bernstein_v._United_States" title="Bernstein v. United States">Bernstein case</a> and the <a href="/wiki/United_States_Court_of_Appeals_for_the_Sixth_Circuit" title="United States Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit">Sixth Circuit Court of Appeals</a> in the <a href="/wiki/Junger_v._Daley" title="Junger v. Daley">Junger case</a>).
</p><p><a href="/wiki/Export_of_cryptography_in_the_United_States#PC_era" class="mw-redirect" title="Export of cryptography in the United States">US export regulations</a> regarding cryptography remain in force, but were liberalized substantially throughout the late 1990s. Since 2000, compliance with the regulations is also much easier. PGP encryption no longer meets the definition of a non-exportable weapon, and can be exported internationally except to seven specific countries and a list of named groups and individuals<sup id="cite&#95;ref-36" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-36"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>36<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> (with whom substantially all US trade is prohibited under various US export controls).
</p>
<div class="mw-heading mw-heading3"><h3 id="PGP_3_and_founding_of_PGP_Inc.">PGP 3 and founding of PGP Inc.</h3><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Pretty_Good_Privacy&amp;action=edit&amp;section=12" title="Edit section: PGP 3 and founding of PGP Inc."><span>edit</span></a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></div>
<p>During this turmoil, Zimmermann's team worked on a new version of PGP encryption called PGP 3. This new version was to have considerable security improvements, including a new certificate structure that fixed small security flaws in the PGP 2.x certificates as well as permitting a certificate to include separate keys for signing and encryption. Furthermore, the experience with patent and export problems led them to eschew patents entirely. PGP 3 introduced the use of the <a href="/wiki/CAST-128" title="CAST-128">CAST-128</a> (a.k.a. CAST5) symmetric key algorithm, and the <a href="/wiki/Digital_Signature_Algorithm" title="Digital Signature Algorithm">DSA</a> and <a href="/wiki/ElGamal" class="mw-redirect" title="ElGamal">ElGamal</a> asymmetric key algorithms, all of which were unencumbered by patents.
</p><p><span class="anchor" id="PGP&#95;Inc"></span>After the Federal criminal investigation ended in 1996, Zimmermann and his team started a company to produce new versions of PGP encryption. They merged with Viacrypt (to whom Zimmermann had sold commercial rights and who had <a href="/wiki/Licensed" class="mw-redirect" title="Licensed">licensed</a> RSA directly from <a href="/wiki/RSADSI" class="mw-redirect" title="RSADSI">RSADSI</a>), which then changed its name to PGP Incorporated. The newly combined Viacrypt/PGP team started work on new versions of PGP encryption based on the PGP 3 system. Unlike PGP 2, which was an exclusively <a href="/wiki/Command_line" class="mw-redirect" title="Command line">command line</a> program, PGP 3 was designed from the start as a <a href="/wiki/Software_library" class="mw-redirect" title="Software library">software library</a> allowing users to work from a command line or inside a <a href="/wiki/GUI" class="mw-redirect" title="GUI">GUI</a> environment. The original agreement between Viacrypt and the Zimmermann team had been that Viacrypt would have even-numbered versions and Zimmermann odd-numbered versions. Viacrypt, thus, created a new version (based on PGP 2) that they called PGP 4. To remove confusion about how it could be that PGP 3 was the successor to PGP 4, PGP 3 was renamed and released as PGP 5 in May 1997.
</p>
<div class="mw-heading mw-heading3"><h3 id="Network_Associates_acquisition">Network Associates acquisition</h3><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Pretty_Good_Privacy&amp;action=edit&amp;section=13" title="Edit section: Network Associates acquisition"><span>edit</span></a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></div>
<p>In December 1997, PGP Inc. was acquired by <a href="/wiki/Network_Associates,_Inc." class="mw-redirect" title="Network Associates, Inc.">Network Associates, Inc.</a> ("NAI"). Zimmermann and the PGP team became NAI employees. NAI was the first company to have a legal export strategy by publishing source code. Under NAI, the PGP team added disk encryption, desktop firewalls, intrusion detection, and <a href="/wiki/IPsec" title="IPsec">IPsec</a> <a href="/wiki/VPN" class="mw-redirect" title="VPN">VPNs</a> to the PGP family. After the export regulation liberalizations of 2000 which no longer required publishing of source, NAI stopped releasing source code.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-37" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-37"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>37<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>
</p>
<div class="mw-heading mw-heading3"><h3 id="Asset_split">Asset split</h3><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Pretty_Good_Privacy&amp;action=edit&amp;section=14" title="Edit section: Asset split"><span>edit</span></a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></div>
<p>In early 2001, Zimmermann left NAI. He served as Chief Cryptographer for <a href="/wiki/Hush_Communications" class="mw-redirect" title="Hush Communications">Hush Communications</a>, who provide an OpenPGP-based e-mail service, <a href="/wiki/Hushmail" title="Hushmail">Hushmail</a>. He has also worked with Veridis and other companies. In October 2001, NAI announced that its PGP assets were for sale and that it was suspending further development of PGP encryption. The only remaining asset kept was the PGP E-Business Server (the original PGP Commandline version).  In February 2002, NAI canceled all support for PGP products, with the exception of the renamed commandline product.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-SDS&#95;38-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-SDS-38"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>38<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup><sup id="cite&#95;ref-39" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-39"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>39<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>
</p>
<div class="mw-heading mw-heading4"><h4 id="McAfee">McAfee</h4><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Pretty_Good_Privacy&amp;action=edit&amp;section=15" title="Edit section: McAfee"><span>edit</span></a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></div>
<p>NAI, now known as <a href="/wiki/McAfee" title="McAfee">McAfee</a>, continued to sell and support the commandline product under the name McAfee E-Business Server until 2013.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-McAfee&#95;40-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-McAfee-40"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>40<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> In 2010, <a href="/wiki/Intel_Corporation" class="mw-redirect" title="Intel Corporation">Intel Corporation</a> acquired <a href="/wiki/McAfee" title="McAfee">McAfee</a>. In 2013, the McAfee E-Business Server was transferred to Software Diversified Services (SDS), which now sells, supports, and develops it under the name SDS E-Business Server.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-McAfee&#95;40-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-McAfee-40"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>40<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup><sup id="cite&#95;ref-SDS&#95;38-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-SDS-38"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>38<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>
</p><p>For the enterprise, Townsend Security currently<sup class="noprint Inline-Template" style="white-space:nowrap;">&#91;<i><a href="/wiki/Wikipedia:Manual_of_Style/Dates_and_numbers#Chronological_items" title="Wikipedia:Manual of Style/Dates and numbers"><span title="The time period mentioned near this tag is ambiguous. (February 2024)">when?</span></a></i>&#93;</sup> offers a commercial version of PGP for the <a href="/wiki/IBM_i" title="IBM i">IBM i</a> and <a href="/wiki/Z/OS" title="Z/OS">IBM z</a> mainframe platforms. Townsend Security partnered with Network Associates in 2000 to create a compatible version of PGP for the IBM i platform. Townsend Security again ported PGP in 2008, this time to the IBM z mainframe. This version of PGP relies on a free z/OS encryption facility, which utilizes hardware acceleration. SDS also offers a commercial version of PGP (SDS E-Business Server) for the <a href="/wiki/Z/OS" title="Z/OS">IBM z</a> mainframe.
</p>
<div class="mw-heading mw-heading4"><h4 id="PGP_Corporation">PGP Corporation</h4><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Pretty_Good_Privacy&amp;action=edit&amp;section=16" title="Edit section: PGP Corporation"><span>edit</span></a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></div>
<p>In August 2002, several ex-PGP team members formed a new company, <a href="/wiki/PGP_Corporation" title="PGP Corporation">PGP Corporation</a>, and bought the PGP assets (except for the command line version) from NAI. The new company was funded by Rob Theis of Doll Capital Management (DCM) and Terry Garnett of Venrock Associates. PGP Corporation supported existing PGP users and honored NAI's support contracts. Zimmermann served as a special advisor and consultant to PGP Corporation while continuing to run his own consulting company. In 2003, PGP Corporation created a new server-based product called PGP Universal. In mid-2004, PGP Corporation shipped its own command line version called PGP Command Line, which integrated with the other PGP Encryption Platform applications. In 2005, PGP Corporation made its first acquisition: the <a href="/wiki/Germany" title="Germany">German</a> software company Glück &amp; Kanja Technology AG,<sup id="cite&#95;ref-41" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-41"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>41<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> which became PGP Deutschland AG.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-42" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-42"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>42<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> In 2010, PGP Corporation acquired Hamburg-based certificate authority TC TrustCenter and its parent company, <a href="/wiki/ChosenSecurity" class="mw-redirect" title="ChosenSecurity">ChosenSecurity</a>, to form its PGP TrustCenter<sup id="cite&#95;ref-43" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-43"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>43<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> division.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-44" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-44"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>44<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>
</p><p>After the 2002 purchase of NAI's PGP assets, PGP Corporation offered worldwide PGP technical support from its offices in <a href="/wiki/Draper,_Utah" title="Draper, Utah">Draper, Utah</a>; <a href="/wiki/Offenbach_am_Main" title="Offenbach am Main">Offenbach</a>, <a href="/wiki/Germany" title="Germany">Germany</a>; and <a href="/wiki/Tokyo" title="Tokyo">Tokyo</a>, Japan.
</p>
<div class="mw-heading mw-heading5"><h5 id="Symantec">Symantec</h5><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Pretty_Good_Privacy&amp;action=edit&amp;section=17" title="Edit section: Symantec"><span>edit</span></a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></div>
<p>On April 29, 2010, <a href="/wiki/NortonLifeLock" class="mw-redirect" title="NortonLifeLock">Symantec Corp.</a> announced that it would acquire PGP Corporation for $300 million with the intent of integrating it into its Enterprise Security Group.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-45" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-45"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>45<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> This acquisition was finalized and announced to the public on June 7, 2010. The source code of PGP Desktop 10 is available for peer review.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-46" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-46"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>46<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>
</p><p>In May 2018, a bug named <a href="/wiki/EFAIL" title="EFAIL">EFAIL</a> was discovered in certain implementations of PGP which from 2003 could reveal the plaintext contents of emails encrypted with it.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-47" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-47"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>47<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup><sup id="cite&#95;ref-48" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-48"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>48<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> The chosen mitigation for this vulnerability in PGP Desktop is to mandate the use <a href="/w/index.php?title=SEIP&amp;action=edit&amp;redlink=1" class="new" title="SEIP (page does not exist)">SEIP</a> protected packets in the ciphertext, which can lead to old emails or other encrypted objects to be no longer decryptable after upgrading to the software version that has the mitigation.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-49" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-49"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>49<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>
</p>
<div class="mw-heading mw-heading5"><h5 id="Broadcom">Broadcom</h5><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Pretty_Good_Privacy&amp;action=edit&amp;section=18" title="Edit section: Broadcom"><span>edit</span></a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></div>
<p>On August 9, 2019, <a href="/wiki/Broadcom_Inc." class="mw-redirect" title="Broadcom Inc.">Broadcom Inc.</a> announced they would be acquiring the Enterprise Security software division of Symantec, which includes PGP Corporation.
</p>
<div class="mw-heading mw-heading2"><h2 id="PGP_Corporation_encryption_applications">PGP Corporation encryption applications</h2><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Pretty_Good_Privacy&amp;action=edit&amp;section=19" title="Edit section: PGP Corporation encryption applications"><span>edit</span></a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></div>
<dl><dd><i>This section describes commercial programs available from <a href="/wiki/PGP_Corporation" title="PGP Corporation">PGP Corporation</a>.  For information on other programs compatible with the <a href="#OpenPGP">OpenPGP</a> specification, see <a href="#External_links">External links</a> below.</i></dd></dl>
<p>While originally used primarily for encrypting the contents of e-mail messages and attachments from a desktop client, PGP products have been diversified since 2002 into a set of encryption applications that can be managed by an optional central policy server.  PGP encryption applications include e-mails and attachments, digital signatures, full disk encryption, file and folder security, protection for IM sessions, batch file transfer encryption, and protection for files and folders stored on network servers and, more recently, encrypted or signed HTTP request/responses by means of a client-side (Enigform) and a server-side (mod openpgp) module. There is also a WordPress plugin available, called wp-enigform-authentication, that takes advantage of the session management features of Enigform with mod_openpgp.
</p><p>The PGP Desktop 9.x family includes PGP Desktop Email, PGP Whole Disk Encryption, and PGP NetShare. Additionally, a number of Desktop bundles are also available. Depending on the application, the products feature desktop e-mail, digital signatures, IM security, whole disk encryption, file, and folder security, encrypted <a href="/wiki/Self-extracting_archive" title="Self-extracting archive">self-extracting archives</a>, and <a href="/wiki/Data_erasure" title="Data erasure">secure shredding</a> of deleted files. Capabilities are licensed in different ways depending on the features required.
</p><p>The PGP Universal Server 2.x management console handles centralized deployment, security policy, policy enforcement, key management, and reporting.  It is used for automated e-mail encryption in the gateway and manages PGP Desktop 9.x clients. In addition to its local <a href="/wiki/Key_server_(cryptographic)" title="Key server (cryptographic)">keyserver</a>, PGP Universal Server works with the PGP public keyserver—called the PGP Global Directory—to find recipient keys. It has the capability of delivering e-mail securely when no recipient key is found via a secure HTTPS browser session.
</p><p>With PGP Desktop 9.x managed by PGP Universal Server 2.x, first released in 2005, all PGP encryption applications are based on a new proxy-based architecture. These newer versions of PGP software eliminate the use of e-mail plug-ins and insulate the user from changes to other desktop applications. All desktop and server operations are now based on security policies and operate in an automated fashion. The PGP Universal server automates the creation, management, and expiration of keys, sharing these keys among all PGP encryption applications.
</p><p>The Symantec PGP platform has now undergone a rename.  PGP Desktop is now known as Symantec Encryption Desktop (SED), and the PGP Universal Server is now known as Symantec Encryption Management Server (SEMS). The current shipping versions are Symantec Encryption Desktop 10.3.0 (Windows and macOS platforms) and Symantec Encryption Server 3.3.2.
</p><p>Also available are PGP Command-Line, which enables command line-based encryption and signing of information for storage, transfer, and backup, as well as the PGP Support Package for BlackBerry which enables RIM BlackBerry devices to enjoy sender-to-recipient messaging encryption.
</p><p>New versions of PGP applications use both OpenPGP and the <a href="/wiki/S/MIME" title="S/MIME">S/MIME</a>, allowing communications with any user of a <a href="/wiki/NIST" class="mw-redirect" title="NIST">NIST</a> specified standard.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-50" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-50"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>50<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>
</p>
<div class="mw-heading mw-heading2"><h2 id="OpenPGP">OpenPGP</h2><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Pretty_Good_Privacy&amp;action=edit&amp;section=20" title="Edit section: OpenPGP"><span>edit</span></a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></div>
<p>Within PGP Inc., there was still concern surrounding patent issues. RSADSI was challenging the continuation of the Viacrypt RSA license to the newly merged firm. The company adopted an informal internal standard that they called "Unencumbered PGP" which would "use no algorithm with licensing difficulties".  Because of PGP encryption's importance worldwide, many wanted to write their own software that would interoperate with PGP 5. Zimmermann became convinced that an <a href="/wiki/Open_standard" title="Open standard">open standard</a> for PGP encryption was critical for them and for the cryptographic community as a whole. In July 1997, PGP Inc. proposed to the <a href="/wiki/IETF" class="mw-redirect" title="IETF">IETF</a> that there be a standard called OpenPGP. They gave the IETF permission to use the name OpenPGP to describe this new standard as well as any program that supported the standard. The IETF accepted the proposal and started the OpenPGP <a href="/wiki/IETF_Working_Group" class="mw-redirect" title="IETF Working Group">Working Group</a>.<sup class="noprint Inline-Template Template-Fact" style="white-space:nowrap;">&#91;<i><a href="/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed" title="Wikipedia:Citation needed"><span title="This paragraph may be based on a Wikipedia editor&#39;s memories of the events. Parts of it may be unverifiable. (July 2025)">citation needed</span></a></i>&#93;</sup>
</p><p>OpenPGP is on the <a href="/wiki/Internet_Standard" title="Internet Standard">Internet Standards Track</a> and is under active development. Many e-mail clients provide OpenPGP-compliant email security as described in RFC 3156. The current specification is RFC 9580 (July 2024), the successor to RFC 4880. RFC 9580 specifies a suite of required algorithms consisting of <a href="/wiki/X25519" class="mw-redirect" title="X25519">X25519</a>, <a href="/wiki/EdDSA#Ed25519" title="EdDSA">Ed25519</a>, <a href="/wiki/SHA-2" title="SHA-2">SHA2-256</a> and <a href="/wiki/Advanced_Encryption_Standard" title="Advanced Encryption Standard">AES-128</a>. In addition to these algorithms, the standard recommends <a href="/wiki/X448" class="mw-redirect" title="X448">X448</a>, <a href="/wiki/EdDSA#Ed448" title="EdDSA">Ed448</a>, <a href="/wiki/SHA-2" title="SHA-2">SHA2-384</a>, <a href="/wiki/SHA-2" title="SHA-2">SHA2-512</a> and <a href="/wiki/Advanced_Encryption_Standard" title="Advanced Encryption Standard">AES-256</a>. Beyond these, many other algorithms are supported.
</p>
<ul><li>PGP
<ul><li><link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1333433106" />RFC&#160;<a rel="nofollow" class="external text" href="https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc1991">1991</a> PGP Message Exchange Formats (obsolete)<sup id="cite&#95;ref-tools.ietf.org&#95;51-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-tools.ietf.org-51"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>51<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup></li></ul></li>
<li>OpenPGP
<ul><li><link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1333433106" />RFC&#160;<a rel="nofollow" class="external text" href="https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc2440">2440</a> OpenPGP Message Format (obsolete)<sup id="cite&#95;ref-tools.ietf.org&#95;51-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-tools.ietf.org-51"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>51<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup></li>
<li><link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1333433106" />RFC&#160;<a rel="nofollow" class="external text" href="https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc4880">4880</a> OpenPGP Message Format (obsolete)</li>
<li><link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1333433106" />RFC&#160;<a rel="nofollow" class="external text" href="https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5581">5581</a> The Camellia Cipher in OpenPGP (obsolete)</li>
<li><link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1333433106" />RFC&#160;<a rel="nofollow" class="external text" href="https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6637">6637</a> Elliptic Curve Cryptography (ECC) in OpenPGP (obsolete)</li>
<li><link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1333433106" />RFC&#160;<a rel="nofollow" class="external text" href="https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9580">9580</a> OpenPGP</li></ul></li>
<li>PGP/MIME
<ul><li><link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1333433106" />RFC&#160;<a rel="nofollow" class="external text" href="https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc2015">2015</a> MIME Security with Pretty Good Privacy (PGP)</li>
<li><link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1333433106" />RFC&#160;<a rel="nofollow" class="external text" href="https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc3156">3156</a> MIME Security with OpenPGP</li></ul></li></ul>
<p>OpenPGP's encryption can ensure the secure delivery of files and messages, as well as provide verification of who created or sent the message using a process called digital signing. The <a href="/wiki/Open_source" title="Open source">open source</a> office suite <a href="/wiki/LibreOffice" title="LibreOffice">LibreOffice</a> implemented document signing with OpenPGP as of version 5.4.0 on Linux.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-52" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-52"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>52<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> Using OpenPGP for communication requires participation by both the sender and recipient. OpenPGP can also be used to secure sensitive files when they are stored in vulnerable places like mobile devices or in the cloud.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-53" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-53"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>53<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>
In late 2023, a schism occurred in the OpenPGP world: IETF's OpenPGP working group decided to choose a "crypto-refresh" update strategy for the RFC 4880 specification, rather than a more gradual "4880bis" path preferred by Werner Koch, author of GnuPG. As a result, Koch took his draft, now abandoned by the workgroup, and forked it into a "LibrePGP" specification.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-LibrePGP&#95;9-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-LibrePGP-9"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>9<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>
</p>
<div class="mw-heading mw-heading3"><h3 id="Implementations">Implementations</h3><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Pretty_Good_Privacy&amp;action=edit&amp;section=21" title="Edit section: Implementations"><span>edit</span></a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></div>
<p>The <a href="/wiki/Free_Software_Foundation" title="Free Software Foundation">Free Software Foundation</a> has developed its own OpenPGP-compliant software suite called <a href="/wiki/GNU_Privacy_Guard" title="GNU Privacy Guard">GNU Privacy Guard</a>, freely available together with all source code under the <a href="/wiki/GNU_General_Public_License" title="GNU General Public License">GNU General Public License</a> and is maintained separately from several <a href="/wiki/Graphical_user_interfaces" class="mw-redirect" title="Graphical user interfaces">graphical user interfaces</a> that interact with the GnuPG library for encryption, decryption, and signing functions (see <a href="/wiki/KGPG" title="KGPG">KGPG</a>, <a href="/wiki/Seahorse_(software)" title="Seahorse (software)">Seahorse</a>, <a href="/wiki/MacGPG" class="mw-redirect" title="MacGPG">MacGPG</a>).<sup class="noprint Inline-Template" style="white-space:nowrap;">&#91;<i><a href="/wiki/Wikipedia:Neutral_point_of_view#Due_and_undue_weight" title="Wikipedia:Neutral point of view"><span title="The material near this tag may be giving undue weight to a viewpoint or idea. (July 2021)">undue weight?</span></a>&#32;&#8211; <a href="/wiki/Talk:Pretty_Good_Privacy#undue" title="Talk:Pretty Good Privacy">discuss</a></i>&#93;</sup> Several other vendors<sup class="noprint Inline-Template" style="white-space:nowrap;">&#91;<i><a href="/wiki/Wikipedia:Citing_sources" title="Wikipedia:Citing sources"><span title="readers expect a neutral list of vendors (July 2021)">specify</span></a></i>&#93;</sup> have also developed OpenPGP-compliant software.
</p><p>The development of an <a href="/wiki/Open_source" title="Open source">open source</a> OpenPGP-compliant library, OpenPGP.js, written in <a href="/wiki/JavaScript" title="JavaScript">JavaScript</a> and supported by the <a href="/wiki/Framework_Programmes_for_Research_and_Technological_Development#Horizon_2020" title="Framework Programmes for Research and Technological Development">Horizon 2020 Framework Programme</a> of the <a href="/wiki/European_Union" title="European Union">European Union</a>,<sup id="cite&#95;ref-54" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-54"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>54<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> has allowed web-based applications to use PGP encryption in the web browser.
</p><p>PGP keys are supported in <a href="/wiki/Mozilla_Thunderbird" title="Mozilla Thunderbird">Mozilla Thunderbird</a> (Built-in in version 78 onwards on PC,<sup id="cite&#95;ref-55" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-55"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>55<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> and with the <a href="/wiki/OpenKeychain" title="OpenKeychain">OpenKeychain</a> app as of version 9 on Android<sup id="cite&#95;ref-56" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-56"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>56<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>), <a href="/wiki/GitHub" title="GitHub">GitHub</a>,<sup id="cite&#95;ref-57" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-57"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>57<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> and <a href="/wiki/GitLab" title="GitLab">GitLab</a>.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-58" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-58"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>58<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>
</p>
<div class="mw-heading mw-heading2"><h2 id="Limitations">Limitations</h2><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Pretty_Good_Privacy&amp;action=edit&amp;section=22" title="Edit section: Limitations"><span>edit</span></a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></div>
<p>With the advancement of cryptography, parts of PGP and OpenPGP have been criticized for being dated:
</p>
<ul><li>The long length of PGP public keys, caused by the use of RSA and additional data other than the actual cryptographic key<sup id="cite&#95;ref-2014&#95;green&#95;59-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-2014_green-59"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>59<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup></li>
<li>Lack of <a href="/wiki/Forward_secrecy" title="Forward secrecy">forward secrecy</a><sup id="cite&#95;ref-2014&#95;green&#95;59-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-2014_green-59"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>59<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup></li>
<li>Use of outdated algorithms by default in several implementations<sup id="cite&#95;ref-2014&#95;green&#95;59-2" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-2014_green-59"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>59<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup></li>
<li>Difficulty for the users to comprehend and poor usability<sup id="cite&#95;ref-2015&#95;marlinspike&#95;29-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-2015_marlinspike-29"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>29<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup></li>
<li>Lack of ubiquity<sup id="cite&#95;ref-2015&#95;marlinspike&#95;29-2" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-2015_marlinspike-29"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>29<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup></li></ul>
<p>In October 2017, the <a href="/wiki/ROCA_vulnerability" title="ROCA vulnerability">ROCA vulnerability</a> was announced, which affects RSA keys generated by buggy Infineon firmware used on <a href="/wiki/Yubikey" class="mw-redirect" title="Yubikey">Yubikey</a> 4 tokens, often used with OpenPGP. Many published PGP keys were found to be susceptible.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-60" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-60"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>60<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> Yubico offers free replacement of affected tokens.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-yubicokeyreplace&#95;61-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-yubicokeyreplace-61"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>61<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>
</p>
